```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Crash data often hold several counts for each site: crashes of each
severity, or of each type. `countreg_mv()` fits one count regression for
each outcome in one model. Each outcome has its own family, mean formula
and distribution-parameter formulas.

This is the direct way to model counts by category. A total and its split
across categories is the other way; see
`vignette("total-allocation-models")`.

```{r setup}
library(flexCountReg)
data("washington_roads")
w <- washington_roads
w$pdo <- w$Total_crashes - w$Injury_crashes
w$injury <- w$Injury_crashes
colSums(w[, c("pdo", "injury")])
```

## 1. One family for each outcome

Outcomes can behave differently. Property damage only (PDO) crashes are
frequent; injury crashes are rarer and can be more skewed. So each
outcome can have its own family:

```{r fit}
m <- countreg_mv(cbind(pdo, injury) ~ lnaadt + speed50 + offset(lnlength),
                 data = w, family = c(pdo = "NB2", injury = "PIG"))
summary(m)
```

The coefficients are named `<outcome>:<term>`. `family` takes one code for
every outcome, or one per outcome. Different right-hand sides are given as
a list of formulas, one per outcome:

```{r formulas}
m2 <- countreg_mv(list(pdo = pdo ~ lnaadt + speed50 + offset(lnlength),
                       injury = injury ~ lnaadt + offset(lnlength)),
                  data = w, family = c(pdo = "NB2", injury = "PIG"))
AIC(m, m2)
```

`dis_param_formula_1` and `dis_param_formula_2` take one formula for every
outcome or a list named by outcome, so the dispersion of one outcome can
depend on covariates while the others stay constant.

## 2. Choosing the families

The equations are fitted together, but in this version they are
independent given the covariates: the log-likelihood is the sum of the
equations' log-likelihoods, and each equation's estimates equal those of a
separate `countreg()` fit. So the family of each outcome can be chosen by
comparing fits that change only that outcome's family:

```{r families}
fams <- list(c("NB2", "NB2"), c("NB2", "PIG"), c("NB2", "PLN"),
             c("PIG", "PIG"))
sapply(fams, function(f) {
  fit <- countreg_mv(cbind(pdo, injury) ~ lnaadt + speed50 +
                       offset(lnlength), data = w, family = f)
  c(pdo = f[1], injury = f[2], AIC = round(AIC(fit), 1))
})
```

Here the choices fit almost equally well (the AICs are within 0.3), so
the simpler NB2 is a reasonable choice for both outcomes. With rarer or
more skewed outcomes the differences between families are larger.

## 3. Tests across equations

One fit gives the covariance of all the estimates, so hypotheses that
involve several equations can be tested. Is the effect of traffic the
same for PDO and injury crashes?

```{r wald}
b <- coef(m)
V <- vcov(m)
a <- c("pdo:lnaadt", "injury:lnaadt")
diff <- b[a[1]] - b[a[2]]
se <- sqrt(V[a[1], a[1]] + V[a[2], a[2]] - 2 * V[a[1], a[2]])
c(difference = unname(diff), z = unname(diff / se),
  p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(unname(diff / se))))
```

Traffic increases PDO crashes clearly more than injury crashes
(p < 0.001), so the share of injury crashes falls as traffic grows. The
covariance between the two estimates is zero here, because the equations
are independent; with correlated equations it would not be.

## 4. Predictions

`predict()` gives a matrix of expected counts, one column per outcome.
`type = "prob"` gives, for each outcome, the probabilities of the counts
0, 1, 2, ..., and `simulate()` draws all outcomes at once:

```{r predict}
nd <- w[c(1, 50, 200), ]
predict(m, newdata = nd)
lapply(predict(m, newdata = nd, type = "prob", max_count = 3), round, 3)
```

`tidy()` has an `outcome` column, and `residuals()`, `fitted()`,
`confint()` and `glance()` work as for other models.

`rootogram()` compares the observed counts of each outcome with its own fitted
distribution, one plot per outcome (`outcome` selects some of them). It
checks the marginal distributions, not the dependence between the outcomes:

```{r rootogram, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.8}
rootogram(m)
```

## 5. Correlated outcomes

The counts of different severity levels at a site are usually correlated:
unobserved conditions that raise PDO crashes also raise injury crashes.
`rpar_formula` adds random parameters to the equations, drawn once per
unit of `group_var` (here a road segment, shared by its three years) and
correlated across equations (`correlation = "across"`, the default).

Poisson outcomes with correlated normal random intercepts give the
**multivariate Poisson-lognormal model** (MVPLN): each segment's
intercepts in the two equations are bivariate normal, which makes each
outcome overdispersed and the two outcomes correlated.

```{r mvpln}
mr <- countreg_mv(cbind(pdo, injury) ~ lnaadt + speed50 + offset(lnlength),
                  data = w, family = "POISSON", rpar_formula = ~ 1,
                  group_var = "ID", rpar_draws = 200, seed = 1)
summary(mr)
AIC(m, mr)
```

The estimated correlation of the random intercepts is about 0.64:
segments with more PDO crashes than their traffic and speed limit predict
tend to have more injury crashes too. The evidence for it is modest (the
`chol:` element that carries it has p of about 0.06), because injury
crashes are rare. The MVPLN still fits much better than the independent
NB2 and PIG equations (AIC 2472 against 2510). Other families can be used in the same way: they keep their
own overdispersion within each outcome, and the random intercepts add the
correlation between outcomes. Random slopes are more terms in
`rpar_formula`, such as `~ 1 + lnaadt`, and `rpar_formula` can also be a
list with a different formula for each outcome.

The likelihood is simulated: each segment's likelihood is averaged over
`rpar_draws` draws of its random parameters (randomly shifted Halton
points), with analytic gradients. The standard deviations are reported as
positive; the correlations come from the off-diagonal elements (`chol:`)
of the Cholesky factor.

## 6. Joint and conditional probabilities

With correlated outcomes, the probability of a combination of counts is
not the product of the outcomes' probabilities. `type = "joint"` gives the
probability of given counts of all outcomes, and `type = "conditional"`
the distribution of one outcome given counts of the others, such as the
chance of injury crashes on a segment-year with three PDO crashes:

```{r conditional}
nd <- w[c(1, 50, 200), ]
predict(mr, newdata = nd, type = "joint", y = c(pdo = 1, injury = 1))
round(predict(mr, newdata = nd, type = "prob", max_count = 2)$injury, 4)
round(predict(mr, newdata = nd, type = "conditional", outcome = "injury",
              given = c(pdo = 3), max_count = 2), 4)
round(predict(mr, newdata = nd, type = "conditional", outcome = "injury",
              given = c(pdo = 0), max_count = 2), 4)
```

Three PDO crashes raise the probability of an injury crash above its
marginal value, and no PDO crash lowers it. Without random parameters (or
a copula, Section 7) the equations are independent, and the conditional
probabilities equal the marginal ones.

For segments in the estimation data, `random = "posterior"` uses their own
crash history (Empirical Bayes):

```{r posterior}
seg <- w[w$ID == w$ID[1], ]
round(cbind(predict(mr, newdata = seg),
            predict(mr, newdata = seg, random = "posterior")), 3)
```

## 7. Copulas

A copula joins the outcomes' own distributions into one joint
distribution, so each outcome keeps its family and its expected counts:

$$
P(Y_1 \le y_1, Y_2 \le y_2) = C\big(F_1(y_1), F_2(y_2); \theta\big).
$$

For counts, the probability of the observed pair is the exact volume of the
copula over the rectangle $[F_1(y_1 - 1), F_1(y_1)] \times
[F_2(y_2 - 1), F_2(y_2)]$, the sum of four copula values (of $2^J$ with $J$
outcomes). For a count far in the upper tail of its distribution both ends
of its interval are within rounding of 1, so there the volume is
integrated over the upper tail probabilities $P(Y > y)$ instead, and
improbable pairs keep their precision. The copula families differ in the
shape of the dependence:

| `copula` | dependence |
|---|---|
| `"gaussian"` | symmetric, any sign, no tail dependence (two outcomes) |
| `"frank"` | symmetric, no tail dependence; any sign for two outcomes |
| `"clayton"` | positive, strongest for joint low counts |
| `"gumbel"` | positive, strongest for joint high counts |

```{r copula}
mc <- countreg_mv(cbind(pdo, injury) ~ lnaadt + speed50 + offset(lnlength),
                  data = w, family = c(pdo = "NB2", injury = "PIG"),
                  copula = "clayton")
summary(mc)
```

`summary()` reports the copula parameter and its Kendall's tau. With
counts, this tau describes the copula, not the rank correlation of the
counts themselves, which is weaker when the counts are small.

Here the copulas barely change the fit, while the MVPLN of section 5 fits
much better:

```{r copula-compare}
fams <- c(pdo = "NB2", injury = "PIG")
f <- cbind(pdo, injury) ~ lnaadt + speed50 + offset(lnlength)
cop <- lapply(c("gaussian", "frank", "clayton", "gumbel"), function(cf)
  countreg_mv(f, data = w, family = fams, copula = cf))
round(c(independent = AIC(m), gaussian = AIC(cop[[1]]),
        frank = AIC(cop[[2]]), clayton = AIC(cop[[3]]),
        gumbel = AIC(cop[[4]]), MVPLN = AIC(mr)))
```

The two models describe different dependence. The copula links the two
counts of the same segment-year; the random intercepts of the MVPLN are shared
by a segment's three years, so it also captures that some segments have
more crashes of both kinds year after year. In these data the dependence
is mostly of the second kind. A copula suits outcomes measured once per
unit, or dependence within a period; random parameters suit repeated
observations of the same units.

The two can also be combined: random intercepts shared by a segment's
years, and a copula for what remains within each year.

```{r both, eval = FALSE}
mb <- countreg_mv(cbind(pdo, injury) ~ lnaadt + speed50 + offset(lnlength),
                  data = w, family = "POISSON", rpar_formula = ~ 1,
                  group_var = "ID", rpar_draws = 200, seed = 1,
                  copula = "frank")
```

This fit takes about two minutes. Its copula parameter is close to zero
(Frank theta 0.06, standard error 0.71), and its AIC (2474.7) is higher
than that of the MVPLN alone (2472.1): once the segments' random
intercepts are in the model, nothing is left for the copula. On simulated
data with both kinds of dependence, the combined model recovers both.

All parameters of a copula model are estimated together by maximum
likelihood (started from the separate equations and the best copula
parameter for them), with analytic gradients from the derivatives of the
copula and of each outcome's distribution function. `predict()` gives joint
and conditional probabilities from the copula, and `simulate()` draws
the outcomes from it.
